a: for the lifetime of the system plus one year after it is withdrawn from service
b: at least six months, unless other Union or national law provides otherwise
c: at least ten years from the date the system was placed on the Union market
d: at least three years, matching the retention period for conformity records
explain: Art 26(6) sets a six-month floor for deployer log retention, appropriate to the intended purpose of the system. The ten-year figure belongs to Art 18, which covers the provider's technical documentation and declaration of conformity.

q: An insurer buys a third-party claims-triage system, markets it under its own brand and retrains it on its own data. Under the value-chain rules the insurer:
a: becomes the provider and takes on the full set of provider obligations
b: shares provider obligations jointly and severally with the original developer
c: stays a deployer but must obtain the original provider's written consent
d: becomes an importer, with the verification duties attached to that role
explain: Art 25(1) shifts provider status to anyone who puts their name or trademark on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification, or changes its purpose so that it becomes high-risk. The original provider must then cooperate and supply information under Art 25(2); liability is not shared jointly.

q: Which deployer must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use of an Annex III system?
a: a private bank scoring consumers for creditworthiness with the system
b: a software vendor placing the system on the market under its own trademark
c: a logistics firm using the system to schedule deliveries across its own fleet
d: a manufacturer using the system as a safety component in its production line
explain: Art 27 binds bodies governed by public law, private operators providing public services, and deployers of the credit-scoring and life and health insurance pricing systems in Annex III points 5(b) and 5(c). A vendor placing a system on the market is a provider, not a deployer, so Art 27 never reaches it.

q: A benefits claimant is refused an allowance after a decision informed by a high-risk system. Art 86 entitles the claimant to:
a: compensation from the deployer where the decision is later found to be wrong
b: a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role in the decision
c: an automatic re-examination of the decision by a human caseworker within 30 days
d: access to the technical documentation and the system's performance test results
explain: Art 86 gives affected persons the right to an explanation of the role the AI system played in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision taken. It creates no re-examination right, which flows from GDPR Art 22(3), and no claim to the provider's documentation.

q: Which of these triggers no Art 50 transparency obligation?
a: A customer-service assistant that answers user queries in natural language
b: A generator producing photorealistic images of an identifiable politician
c: An internal spam filter that silently quarantines suspicious inbound mail
d: A tool producing synthetic audio published as part of a news programme
explain: Art 50 covers disclosure when a person interacts with an AI system, machine-readable marking of synthetic content, deepfake disclosure, and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. A spam filter is minimal risk and carries no transparency duty.

q: As amended by the Digital Omnibus, the Art 4 AI literacy duty requires providers and deployers to:
a: appoint an AI literacy officer responsible for annual training of all system users
b: ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff, verified by documented testing
c: take measures supporting AI literacy among staff and others operating their systems
d: certify their AI operators against a recognised European competence framework
explain: The rewritten Art 4 is an obligation of effort: measures to support the development of AI literacy, expressly without any duty to guarantee a specific level. The pre-Omnibus text spoke of ensuring a sufficient level, which is exactly what makes the stricter reading tempting.

q: A general-purpose model is presumed to carry systemic risk once cumulative training compute exceeds:
a: 10^23 floating-point operations, with the count reset on each new model generation
b: 10^24 floating-point operations, measured across pre-training and fine-tuning combined
c: 10^25 floating-point operations, a figure the Commission may adjust by delegated act
d: 10^26 floating-point operations, counting only the final pre-training run of the model
explain: Art 51(2) sets the 10^25 FLOP presumption and Art 51(3) allows the Commission to amend the threshold by delegated act; Annex XIII criteria permit designation even below it. Providers must notify the Commission within two weeks under Art 52.

q: A provider releases a new general-purpose model below the systemic-risk threshold. Its baseline obligations are:
a: model evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting and infrastructure cybersecurity
b: technical documentation, downstream information, a copyright policy and training summary
c: notification to the Commission, an external audit and publication of evaluation results
d: registration in the EU database, CE marking and a declaration of conformity for the model
explain: Art 53(1) lists the four baseline duties for every GPAI model provider, the training-content summary following the AI Office template published in July 2025. Evaluation and red-teaming are Art 55 duties reserved for systemic-risk models, and models are never CE-marked.

q: A model released under a free and open licence with public weights and parameters is still bound by:
a: the technical documentation duty, from which no GPAI provider is ever released
b: the copyright policy and the training-content summary, with no exemption
c: the downstream information duty owed to providers integrating the model
d: the systemic-risk duties, which attach to every openly released model
explain: Art 53(2) exempts free and open-licence models from the technical documentation and downstream information duties only, and that exemption disappears entirely for models with systemic risk. The copyright policy and training-content summary under Art 53(1) always apply.

q: A model crosses the systemic-risk threshold. Beyond the baseline duties, its provider must:
a: secure Commission authorisation before release and publish the complete evaluation report
b: evaluate the model, mitigate systemic risk, report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity
c: submit the model to a notified body and affix a CE mark before making it available in the Union
d: register the model in the EU database and appoint an independent external safety auditor
explain: Art 55(1) adds four duties: state-of-the-art evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure. No prior authorisation or CE marking exists for models.

q: What is the legal status of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice published in July 2025?
a: voluntary, offering an adequate way to demonstrate compliance pending harmonised standards
b: binding on all GPAI providers once the Commission confirmed its adequacy by implementing act
c: binding only on providers of models presenting systemic risk, the rest remaining voluntary
d: an interpretive guideline with no compliance value, superseded by the AI Office templates
explain: Signature is voluntary, and adherence gives providers a recognised route to show compliance with Arts 53 and 55 until harmonised standards exist; the Commission and the Board confirmed its adequacy. Only the Safety and Security chapter targets systemic-risk providers, which does not make it binding, and models on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027.

q: A GPAI provider's copyright policy must in particular identify and respect reservations of rights expressed under:
a: Art 4(3) of the DSM Copyright Directive, the text-and-data-mining opt-out
b: Art 5 of the InfoSoc Directive, listing exceptions to the reproduction right
c: Art 3 of the same Directive, covering mining by research organisations
d: the sui generis database right, as extended to AI training data by case law
explain: Art 53(1)(c) requires state-of-the-art technologies to identify and comply with rights reservations made under Art 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. The Art 3 exception for scientific research by research organisations cannot be opted out of, so it is not the hook for commercial training.

q: A national authority suspects a GPAI model's training-data summary is inadequate. Enforcement of that duty sits with:
a: the European AI Board, which coordinates enforcement across all the Member States
b: the Commission, acting through the AI Office, which alone supervises GPAI models
c: the national market surveillance authority of the Member State where harm occurred
d: the notified body that assessed the model before it was made available in the Union
explain: Arts 88 and 101 give the Commission, acting through the AI Office, exclusive powers over Chapter V GPAI obligations, with fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover. National market surveillance authorities enforce everything else and may ask the AI Office to act.

q: The European Artificial Intelligence Board is composed of:
a: the heads of the national market surveillance authorities and of notified bodies
b: one representative per Member State, with the EDPS attending as an observer
c: independent scientific experts appointed by the Commission for renewable terms
d: representatives of industry, academia, SMEs and civil society organisations
explain: Art 65 provides for one representative per Member State, the EDPS as observer, and the AI Office attending without voting rights. Stakeholders sit in the Advisory Forum under Art 67 and independent experts in the scientific panel under Art 68.

q: The scientific panel of independent experts supports enforcement chiefly by:
a: issuing qualified alerts to the AI Office about systemic risks of GPAI models
b: certifying the evaluation methodologies used by providers of frontier models
c: imposing interim measures on providers pending a Commission investigation
d: adopting the harmonised standards on which the presumption of conformity rests
explain: Art 68 establishes the panel, which advises the AI Office and can trigger a qualified alert under Art 90 where a model may present a concrete systemic risk. It holds no enforcement or standard-setting power; harmonised standards come from CEN-CENELEC.

q: A Member State implementing the Act must designate, as a minimum:
a: its data protection authority, which the Act designates for all high-risk supervision
b: one national AI agency combining supervision, certification and sandbox administration
c: one notifying authority and one market surveillance authority, plus a contact point
d: one notified body per Annex III area, accredited by the national accreditation body
explain: Art 70(1) requires at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority, one of them acting as single point of contact; the deadline was 2 August 2025 and several Member States missed it. Under Art 74(8) Member States designate either the data protection supervisory authority or another authority meeting the conditions of Arts 41 to 44 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, and only for the Annex III point 1 law-enforcement, border-management and justice uses and Annex III points 6, 7 and 8.

q: Under the Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus, AI regulatory sandboxes:
a: must be operational in every Member State by 2 August 2026, run jointly where preferred
b: are optional for Member States, the Commission operating a single Union sandbox instead
c: must be operational in every Member State by 2 August 2027, with an optional EU-level one
d: are reserved for providers of general-purpose models with systemic risk and their partners
explain: The Omnibus moved the Art 57 national sandbox deadline from 2 August 2026 to 2 August 2027 and added a Union-level sandbox that the AI Office may establish, with priority access for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps. The 2026 date is the pre-Omnibus rule that outdated materials still repeat.

q: The top penalty bracket in the AI Act, reserved for prohibited practices, is:
a: EUR 15 million or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
b: EUR 20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
c: EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
d: EUR 7.5 million or 1% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
explain: Art 99(3) sets EUR 35 million or 7% for breaches of Art 5. Most other operator infringements attract EUR 15 million or 3%, and supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities EUR 7.5 million or 1%; the 4% figure belongs to the GDPR.

q: An EU agency is found to have used a prohibited AI practice. The fine would be imposed by:
a: the European Data Protection Supervisor, up to EUR 1.5 million
b: the Commission acting through the AI Office, up to EUR 35 million
c: the market surveillance authority of the Member State hosting it
d: the Court of Justice, on an application made by the Commission
explain: Art 100 empowers the EDPS to fine Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies - up to EUR 1.5 million for prohibited practices and EUR 750 000 for other breaches. National authorities and the AI Office have no jurisdiction over Union bodies.

q: After the Digital Omnibus, obligations for stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems start to apply on:
a: 2 February 2027, six months after the Omnibus entered into force in the Union
b: 2 August 2026, the Omnibus having left the high-risk calendar untouched
c: 2 August 2028, the same date as Annex I product-embedded high-risk systems
d: 2 December 2027, a fixed date replacing the original 2 August 2026
explain: Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 fixed 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I embedded systems, replacing the earlier staggered scheme. Material still quoting 2 August 2026 for high-risk obligations predates the Omnibus.

q: A company has run a public-facing generative chatbot since 2024. Under the Act as amended, its duty to mark the chatbot's synthetic outputs in machine-readable form bites on:
a: 2 August 2026, the general Art 50 date, with no transitional arrangement
b: 27 July 2026, the date the Digital Omnibus itself entered into force in the Union
c: 2 December 2027, aligned with the deferred Annex III high-risk obligations
d: 2 December 2026, a grace period applying to systems already on the market
explain: Art 50 kept its 2 August 2026 date through the Omnibus, so the Art 50(1) duty to tell users they are interacting with AI applies from then with no transition. Art 111(4), inserted by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, gives systems generating synthetic content that were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 to comply with Art 50(2). Systems placed on the market on or after 2 August 2026 get no transition.

q: A deployer of a hiring model wants to process applicants' ethnicity data solely to measure and correct bias. The AI Act now:
a: permits this only where each applicant has given explicit and separate consent
b: prohibits this, bias testing being confined to synthetic or anonymised data
c: permits this under Art 10(5), but only for providers of high-risk AI systems
d: permits this under Art 4a, subject to strict necessity and specific safeguards
explain: The Omnibus deleted Art 10(5) and replaced it with Art 4a, extending the bias-detection gateway to providers and deployers of AI systems and models rather than high-risk providers alone. It remains conditional: no effective alternative such as synthetic or anonymised data, state-of-the-art security, strict access controls, no transmission to third parties, deletion after correction, and documented justification.

q: How do the AI Act and the GDPR interact for a high-risk system processing personal data?
a: a CE-marked system is presumed to comply with the GDPR for its declared intended purpose
b: the GDPR applies only where no conformity assessment has been carried out for the system
c: the Act is lex specialis and displaces the GDPR for AI-related processing operations
d: in parallel: the Act adds product duties, the GDPR governs processing lawfulness
explain: Art 2(7) preserves Union data protection law in full: a compliant high-risk system still needs a lawful basis, and the Art 27 FRIA can build on an existing DPIA under Art 27(4). CE marking certifies product requirements and says nothing about data protection compliance.

q: An energy operator deploys an AI system for grid balancing. Art 15 of the AI Act and NIS2 differ in that:
a: Art 15 secures the entity's networks, while NIS2 applies to individual software products
b: Art 15 applies only to GPAI models, while NIS2 covers deployed high-risk AI systems
c: Art 15 binds providers established in the Union, while NIS2 covers third-country firms
d: Art 15 secures the AI product itself, while NIS2 secures the entity and its networks
explain: Art 15 is product-level accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity for the high-risk system; NIS2 imposes organisational risk-management and incident-reporting duties on essential and important entities. Compliance with the Cyber Resilience Act can support, but never replaces, the Art 15 assessment.

q: Following the withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive, civil liability for harm caused by a defective AI system rests mainly on:
a: the AI Act's own Art 99 penalties, which an injured party may invoke directly
b: national tort law alone, no Union instrument covering damage caused by software
c: the Machinery Regulation, wherever the AI is embedded in a physical product
d: the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which counts software and AI as products
explain: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 brings software and AI systems within the product definition, imposing strict liability for defect with disclosure duties and rebuttable presumptions of defectiveness and causation. The fault-based AI Liability Directive was announced for withdrawal in the Commission's work programme of February 2025 and the withdrawal was formally published in the Official Journal on 6 October 2025 (C/2025/5423).

q: The Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI of the High-Level Expert Group set out seven requirements, among them:
a: patentability of models, portability of weights and interoperability of interfaces
b: proportionality of cost, market scalability and demonstrable return on investment
c: certification by an accredited body, insurance cover and mandatory incident reporting
d: societal and environmental well-being, and diversity, non-discrimination and fairness
explain: The seven are human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; and accountability. In that framework trustworthy AI is lawful, ethical and robust.

q: An organisation wants a certifiable management system for its AI activities, auditable like its existing information-security certification. The right standard is:
a: ISO/IEC 22989, which defines AI terminology and lifecycle concepts
b: ISO/IEC 23894, which gives guidance on managing risk in AI activities
c: ISO/IEC 25059, which sets out a quality model for AI-based systems
d: ISO/IEC 42001, specifying requirements for an AI management system
explain: ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable AI management system standard, structured on the same harmonised clauses as ISO/IEC 27001. ISO/IEC 23894 is guidance on AI risk management that cannot be certified against, which is what makes it the tempting near-miss.

q: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises its core around which functions?
a: Assess, Mitigate, Certify and Monitor, mirroring conformity assessment steps
b: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, applied to AI-specific assets
c: Plan, Do, Check and Act, aligned with the management-system standards cycle
d: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with Govern cutting across the other three
explain: Govern is the cross-cutting function, while Map, Measure and Manage run through context, analysis and response; the Generative AI Profile of July 2024 applies them to general-purpose models. The five-function list is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, a deliberate near-miss.

q: An online lender approves or refuses credit with no human involvement at any point. Under the GDPR this is:
a: prohibited outright, solely automated decisions on credit never being permissible at all
b: outside Art 22, which covers only profiling that leads to special-category inferences
c: permitted provided the privacy notice explains the logic of the decision-making involved
d: restricted by Art 22, needing contract, Union or Member State law, or explicit consent
explain: Art 22(1) restricts decisions based solely on automated processing producing legal or similarly significant effects, Art 22(2) opens three gateways, and Art 22(3) requires safeguards including human intervention, expression of a view and contestation. The AI Act's Art 86 explanation right sits alongside this, not instead of it.

q: A hospital's triage system begins mis-ranking a patient group and the deployer concludes it now presents a risk. It must:
a: notify the notified body that certified the system and await its corrective instruction
b: suspend use and inform the provider and the market surveillance authority without delay
c: retrain the model on corrected data before notifying anyone outside the organisation
d: log the anomaly and raise it in the next scheduled post-market monitoring review cycle
explain: Art 26(5) requires deployers to suspend use and inform the provider, and where a serious incident has occurred to report it under Art 73. Post-market monitoring is the provider's system under Art 72 and cannot absorb a live risk on the deployer's side.

q: For how long must a high-risk provider keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity available to authorities?
a: 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service
b: for as long as the system remains in use, plus 3 years after withdrawal
c: 5 years after the last unit of the system was supplied on the Union market
d: 6 months after the system is placed on the market or put into service
explain: Arts 18 and 47 both set ten years from placing on the market or putting into service, for the documentation and for the declaration respectively. Six months is the deployer's log-retention floor under Art 26(6), which is the classic confusion.

q: Enforcement against non-compliant AI systems draws its procedural framework from:
a: Reg. (EU) 2019/1020 on market surveillance and compliance of products
b: Reg. (EU) 2023/1230, the Machinery Regulation, for all embedded AI systems
c: Directive 2001/95/EC on general product safety, as recast in 2023 for software
d: Reg. (EU) 2022/2065, the Digital Services Act, and its enforcement chapter
explain: Art 74(1) applies Reg. (EU) 2019/1020 to AI systems within scope, which is where authorities find their investigation and corrective powers. Art 77 additionally lets fundamental-rights bodies request documentation about rights-relevant high-risk systems.

q: A company builds a customer chatbot on a licensed general-purpose model that carries systemic risk. Which statement is accurate?
a: the chatbot escapes Art 50 because the model provider already marks its own outputs
b: the model carries Chapter V duties while the chatbot is classified on its own
c: the company becomes a provider of the model by integrating it into its own product
d: the chatbot inherits high-risk status because the underlying model has systemic risk
explain: Model-level and system-level tracks run in parallel: Arts 53 and 55 bind the model provider, while the chatbot is classified by its own intended purpose and owes Art 50 disclosure as a system people interact with. Integration alone does not make the integrator a model provider.

q: How are administrative fines calculated for an SME or a small mid-cap company?
a: only the fixed amounts apply, turnover percentages being reserved for large firms
b: the same brackets apply, but capped at the lower of the percentage or fixed amount
c: fines are replaced by corrective measures unless the infringement is a repeat one
d: the same brackets apply, but reduced by half for a first infringement of the Act
explain: Art 99(6) caps SME and start-up fines at the lower of the two figures rather than the higher. The Omnibus added Art 99(6a) giving small mid-caps — fewer than 750 staff and turnover up to EUR 150 million or balance sheet up to EUR 129 million under Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 — the same lower cap, but only for the paragraph 4 and 5 brackets; a small mid-cap breaching Art 5 still faces the full EUR 35 million or 7%.

q: A provider's training run will cross the systemic-risk compute threshold. It must inform the Commission:
a: before the training run starts, in an ex ante notification to the AI Office
b: in the annual transparency report submitted to the AI Office each January
c: without delay and in any event within two weeks of that becoming known
d: without delay and in any event within two months of that becoming known
explain: Art 52(1) requires notification without delay and at the latest within two weeks of the requirement being met, or of it becoming known that it will be met. The provider may argue exceptionally that its model presents no systemic risk, but it must still notify first.

q: An EU institution is tendering for a high-risk AI system it will deploy. The most effective way to make the Act's obligations enforceable against the winning supplier is to:
a: require delivery of the model weights and the full training dataset upon acceptance
b: make the award conditional on the supplier having signed the GPAI Code of Practice
c: adopt the EU model contractual clauses for AI procurement, mapping duties into terms
d: rely on the supplier's general warranty that it complies with all applicable Union law
explain: The EU model contractual AI clauses, maintained by the Public Buyers Community with Commission support, exist in a high-risk and a light version and turn documentation, logging, oversight and change-notification duties into contract terms with remedies. A bare compliance warranty leaves the buyer with no evidence trail and no enforcement hook.

q: An EU agency wants to fine-tune a model on personal data from its own case files. The lawfulness of that processing is governed by:
a: Directive (EU) 2016/680, covering processing by competent public authorities
b: the AI Act as lex specialis, the processing serving an AI training purpose
c: Reg. (EU) 2018/1725, which applies data protection rules to Union bodies
d: Reg. (EU) 2016/679, since the agency acts as a controller within the Union
explain: Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies fall outside the GDPR; Reg. (EU) 2018/1725 is their regime, supervised by the EDPS. The GDPR answer tempts because the substantive rules are nearly identical, but the applicable instrument decides who supervises and which lawful bases are available.

q: A controller relies on legitimate interest to train a model on web-scraped personal data. Under EDPB Opinion 28/2024 the balancing turns most heavily on:
a: whether a data protection impact assessment was completed before scraping began
b: whether cumulative training compute stays below the systemic-risk threshold
c: data subjects' reasonable expectations and the mitigations the controller applied
d: whether the resulting model is released open-weight rather than as a hosted API
explain: The Opinion applies the three-step test from Guidelines 1/2024 and puts the decisive weight in the third step: reasonable expectations plus mitigating measures, assessed case by case. A completed DPIA is a separate obligation and does not by itself make the interest override.

q: When may a trained model itself be treated as falling outside data protection law?
a: never, any model derived from personal data inheriting the character of that data
b: where extraction or regurgitation is not possible by means reasonably likely to be used
c: only where it was trained exclusively on synthetic or fully aggregated source data
d: always, since a model stores statistical parameters rather than records of individuals
explain: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 treats anonymity as an evidenced, case-by-case conclusion resting on a negligible likelihood of extracting personal data from the model or obtaining it through outputs, judged by all means reasonably likely to be used. Being made only of weights is not itself an argument.

q: A Commission service wants to send documents containing personal data to a US-hosted model API. The governing question is primarily:
a: Chapter V transfer rules: adequacy, or safeguards plus a transfer assessment
b: the Cyber Resilience Act's requirements for products with digital elements
c: the Data Act's rules on switching between data-processing service providers
d: Art 50 of the AI Act, through its transparency duties for generated content
explain: Sending personal data to a third-country API is an international transfer requiring an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, and in practice a transfer impact assessment. The AI Act contains no transfer regime at all, which is why the Art 50 option is a plausible-looking dead end.

q: You must design a benchmark measuring whether a general-purpose model poses a specific capability risk. What most distinguishes a usable risk benchmark from a marketing score?
a: construct validity and an uncontaminated held-out split, reported with uncertainty
b: a large item count, so that per-item noise averages out over the whole evaluation
c: scoring by a larger frontier model as judge rather than by trained human raters
d: full publication of every item, so that providers can optimise against one target
explain: A risk benchmark is decision-grade only if it measures the construct it claims to, on data the model has not seen, with per-capability results and error bars. Publishing every item invites contamination and Goodharting, which is precisely how a benchmark decays into a marketing number.

q: An audit requires that an AI-assisted decision taken six months ago be reproducible. The minimum to version and retain is:
a: the training dataset and the model weights as they stood at the time of the decision
b: model version, the exact prompt, the retrieved context and the decoding parameters
c: the user's original question together with the final answer that was returned to them
d: the application source code, the container image digest and the server access logs
explain: With a hosted model you cannot pin the weights, so reproducibility depends on pinning the whole input state: model version, prompt, retrieved chunks, sampling parameters and any tool outputs. Source code and access logs record what ran, not what the model was given.

q: A deployer claims it satisfies the Art 86 explanation right by showing affected persons a feature-attribution plot of the five strongest drivers. The main weakness is:
a: the explanation must be produced by a notified body rather than by the deployer
b: a local attribution explains the output, not the system's role in the procedure
c: attribution methods are defined for neural networks only, not for tree ensembles
d: feature attributions are trade secrets that cannot lawfully be disclosed outside
explain: Art 86 asks for a clear and meaningful account of the role the system played in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision, in terms the person can act on. A saliency chart may feed into that, but it answers a different question.

q: A caseworker may override the model's recommendation but approves 99% of them within three seconds. The core failure is:
a: automation bias: oversight that is nominal, which the design itself must counter
b: absence of CE marking, without which the system should not be in operation at all
c: insufficient accuracy, which is why the caseworker finds nothing left to correct
d: a record-keeping breach, three seconds leaving no usable audit trail behind it
explain: Art 14(4)(b) expressly requires oversight measures that keep the person aware of the tendency to over-rely on outputs, particularly where the system informs decisions about natural persons. Rubber-stamping means the measure exists on paper but is not effective, which is what the Article demands.

q: A large public administration is implementing Art 4 across 20 000 staff. The approach that best fits the obligation is:
a: role-differentiated measures, from awareness for users to deeper training for overseers
b: publication of an internal register of AI systems with owners and risk classifications
c: one mandatory e-learning module for all staff, repeated annually and tracked centrally
d: certification of the organisation against an AI management system standard covering skills
explain: Art 4 requires measures that take account of technical knowledge, experience, education and training, and of the context in which the systems are used, so proportionality by role is the whole point. A single uniform course ignores that, and a management-system certificate evidences process rather than literacy.

q: A border agency runs face matching at a single global decision threshold. The most serious fairness problem is:
a: facial embeddings become biometric data only once a match above threshold returns
b: matching latency will differ measurably across demographic groups at that threshold
c: false-match and false-non-match rates diverge across groups at a fixed threshold
d: global thresholds are among the practices prohibited outright by Art 5 of the Act
explain: Demographic differentials in error rates at a fixed operating point are the documented failure mode in face recognition testing, and they distribute the burden of errors unequally. Nothing in Art 5 bans a global threshold as such: biometric identification at a border is high-risk, not prohibited.

q: An AI governance lead already holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification and now needs a process for identifying and treating AI-specific risks. The natural companion document is:
a: ISO/IEC 27001, the requirements standard for information security management
b: ISO 9001, the generic quality management requirements standard for suppliers
c: ISO/IEC 23894, guidance on AI risk management aligned with ISO 31000
d: ISO/IEC 42005, which covers records of processing for machine-learning models
explain: ISO/IEC 23894 gives AI-specific risk management guidance built on the ISO 31000 structure and is designed to sit under an ISO/IEC 42001 management system. ISO/IEC 42005 exists but concerns AI system impact assessment, not records of processing, which is what makes it a convincing wrong answer.

q: In a three-lines model applied to AI governance, independently validating a deployed model and challenging the owning team's risk assessment belongs to:
a: the first line, the business unit that owns and runs the model
b: an external notified body appointed under the AI Act procedures
c: the second line, the independent risk and compliance function
d: the third line, internal audit reporting to the audit committee
explain: The second line sets the framework and independently challenges and validates what the first line builds and operates, while the third line audits whether both are working rather than doing the validation itself. Notified bodies assess conformity of certain high-risk systems, a different exercise entirely.

q: A group discovers 140 AI uses across its business units, none of them centrally recorded. The first governance control to put in place is:
a: an annual independent audit of the highest-risk systems in the AI portfolio
b: a board-approved risk appetite statement with quantitative tolerance limits
c: an AI inventory recording owner, purpose, risk tier and data for each use
d: a mandatory approval gate blocking every new AI project until it is reviewed
explain: You cannot classify, assign ownership or assess risk against systems you have not enumerated, and both the Art 26 deployer duties and the Art 27 FRIA presuppose knowing which systems you run. Risk appetite and approval gates are sound next steps, but they operate on an inventory.

q: A city deploys an Annex III system to allocate social housing. Which assessment obligation applies?
a: both a data protection impact assessment and a fundamental rights assessment
b: a fundamental rights impact assessment only, which absorbs the data protection one
c: neither, both duties falling on the provider that placed the system on the market
d: a data protection impact assessment only, the city not being a private operator
explain: The city is a body governed by public law deploying an Annex III system, so Art 27 applies, while a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects triggers GDPR Art 35. Art 27(4) lets the FRIA complement and build on an existing DPIA, but it does not replace it.

q: A Union agency deploys a high-risk AI system for staff selection. Which body acts as its market surveillance authority?
a: the market surveillance authority of the Member State hosting the agency's seat
b: the European Data Protection Supervisor, for Union bodies in the Act's scope
c: the European Ombudsman, on complaint by an affected candidate or staff member
d: the AI Office, which supervises all AI used by the Union's own administration
explain: Art 74 designates the EDPS as market surveillance authority for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the Act, excluding the Court of Justice acting in its judicial capacity. The EDPS also holds the power to fine Union bodies under Art 100, so supervision and sanction sit in the same hands.

q: A Commission official wants to paste a draft internal note into a publicly available chatbot to tighten the wording. Under the Commission's staff guidelines on online generative AI tools this is:
a: allowed, provided the output is not copied verbatim into any public document
b: not allowed, as only information already in the public domain may be entered
c: not allowed, staff being barred from using such tools for any work purpose at all
d: allowed, provided the note carries no personal data of identifiable individuals
explain: The guidelines bar staff from entering any non-public information or personal data into publicly available generative AI tools, and separately forbid reproducing outputs verbatim in public documents. Stripping out personal data is not enough, because the confidentiality restriction is wider than data protection, and the tools are not banned outright.

q: Twelve months after deployment, a provider sees its high-risk system's precision fall as the client population shifts. The Act addresses this through:
a: Art 72, the post-market monitoring system and plan the provider runs
b: Art 43, requiring a fresh conformity assessment every twelve months of use
c: Art 61, which governs informed consent for testing in real-world conditions
d: Art 17, the quality management system the notified body re-audits each year
explain: Art 72 obliges providers to collect and analyse performance data across the system's lifetime under a documented plan, feeding the Art 9 risk management process and triggering corrective action under Art 20. A substantial modification would require reassessment, but ordinary drift is monitored, not re-certified on a calendar.

q: A ministry signs a five-year contract for a model-backed document service. Which clause does most to limit lock-in?
a: version pinning with notice, and export of prompts, data and tuning artefacts
b: a most-favoured-customer pricing clause benchmarked against comparable buyers
c: a service credit regime tied to monthly availability and response-time targets
d: a commitment that the supplier will not train on the ministry's data or outputs
explain: Exit cost is driven by whether the buyer can leave with the assets that make the service work, and by protection against silent model changes mid-term. Availability credits, pricing benchmarks and no-training commitments are all worth having, but none of them makes switching supplier feasible.

q: An audit shows a screening model is well calibrated within each group but has unequal false-negative rates between them. The correct reading is:
a: calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold when base rates differ
b: calibration within groups is the accepted legal definition of fairness in the Union
c: the model is biased and recalibrating it per group will equalise the error rates
d: unequal false-negative rates always indicate that a protected attribute was used
explain: This is the impossibility result: where base rates differ, a classifier cannot simultaneously be calibrated within groups and equalised on false-positive and false-negative rates, so choosing a criterion is a judgement about which harm matters more. Neither recalibration nor dropping the protected attribute dissolves the trade-off.

q: The AI Act is a regulation, yet its enforcement stalled in several Member States during 2025-26. The reason was that:
a: Member States must designate and resource notifying and market surveillance authorities, and many did so late
b: the Court of Justice suspended the Regulation's application pending a challenge to its chosen legal basis
c: national parliaments still had to transpose the Regulation into domestic law before it could bind providers
d: the Regulation's prohibitions were held in abeyance until harmonised standards were cited in the Official Journal
explain: A regulation applies directly, but Chapter VII still requires each Member State to designate and equip notifying and market surveillance authorities; by 2026 only a minority had both in place. Transposition is not the issue — a regulation needs none, unlike NIS2.

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026. Its central effect on the AI Act was to:
a: transfer enforcement of the general-purpose AI chapter from the Commission to national market surveillance authorities
b: bring the transparency obligations for synthetic content forward so that they applied from the date of entry into force
c: defer application of the high-risk obligations while leaving the prohibitions and the general-purpose AI chapter in place
d: repeal the high-risk chapter and put a voluntary conformity scheme in its place for Annex III systems
explain: The Omnibus pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028, while Article 5 and Chapter V continued to apply. Deferral is not repeal: conformity assessment remains mandatory once the new dates arrive.

q: Besides Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 itself, the Digital Omnibus on AI amended:
a: the EASA Basic Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230
b: the Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868 and the Data Act (EU) 2023/2854
c: the Digital Services Act (EU) 2022/2065 and the Digital Markets Act (EU) 2022/1925
d: the Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 and the NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555
explain: The Omnibus realigned sectoral product legislation — aviation and machinery — whose AI provisions referenced the original high-risk dates. The data and platform acquis was not touched by this instrument.

q: The 'small mid-cap' category now referred to in the AI Act:
a: applies only to providers of general-purpose AI models that stay below the systemic-risk compute threshold
b: was introduced by the Data Act and determines which providers get priority access to regulatory sandboxes
c: was created by the AI Act itself and covers any provider employing fewer than 250 persons in the Union
d: was defined in Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 and applied to the AI Act by the Digital Omnibus
explain: The category comes from the Commission's 2025 simplification agenda — an enterprise that is not an SME, employs fewer than 750 people and stays under €150 million turnover or €129 million balance sheet — and reached the AI Act only through Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Fewer than 250 employees is the SME ceiling, not the small mid-cap one.

q: A manufacturer wants to use sensor data from machines it has sold to train a predictive-maintenance model. The instrument that most directly governs whether the machines' users can obtain that same data is:
a: the GDPR, which lets data subjects obtain personal data concerning them in a structured machine-readable format
b: the Data Act, which gives users of connected products access to the data they generate and rights to share it
c: the AI Act, which requires providers of high-risk systems to use relevant and representative training data
d: the Data Governance Act, which sets the conditions for re-use of protected public sector data holdings
explain: The Data Act's core right, applicable since 12 September 2025, is user access to connected-product data and onward sharing with third parties of the user's choice. Portability under the GDPR is the closest alternative but covers only personal data of the data subject, whereas machine telemetry is largely non-personal industrial data.

q: The Data Act's chapter on data-processing services obliges providers to:
a: notify the Commission of every processing operation carried out on behalf of a public sector customer
b: remove contractual, commercial and technical obstacles to switching, and phase out switching charges
c: obtain authorisation from the national market surveillance authority before offering services in a Member State
d: keep all data belonging to customers established in the Union stored and processed on Union territory
explain: Switching and interoperability are the Data Act's answer to cloud lock-in, with switching charges withdrawn after a transition period. Data localisation was deliberately not adopted — the Act addresses portability, and separately restricts unlawful third-country access to non-personal data held in the Union.

q: The Data Governance Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/868) established:
a: a single European register of all personal data processing carried out by public sector bodies
b: mandatory open licensing of every category of public sector information held by national administrations
c: a right for users to access the data generated by the connected products they own, rent or lease
d: notification regimes for data intermediation services and for recognised data altruism organisations
explain: The DGA is the trust framework: neutral intermediaries, altruistic data donation, and conditions for re-using protected public sector data. Connected-product access rights belong to the Data Act, adopted a year later, which is the usual confusion.

q: Common European data spaces are best described as:
a: national data registers that Member States are required to notify to the Commission under the Data Act
b: sector-specific federated ecosystems in which participants share data under common governance and interoperability rules
c: centralised Union repositories into which sectoral data is pooled and which the Commission operates under a single access regime
d: certified cloud regions in which service providers must host all data originating within the Union
explain: Data spaces are federated by design: data stays with its holders and is shared under agreed rules, with the European Health Data Space the first one put into legislation. There is no central Commission-run pool — that model was rejected as unworkable for sensitive sectoral data.

q: For a research team seeking EU-wide health data to train a clinical model, the European Health Data Space matters mainly because it:
a: makes approval by a research ethics committee sufficient for cross-border transfers of clinical records
b: removes the need for a lawful basis under data-protection law where the purpose of processing is research
c: creates a permit-based secondary-use regime run by health data access bodies, phased in from around 2029
d: obliges hospitals to publish anonymised patient records in an openly accessible repository from 2027
explain: The EHDS builds a governed route to secondary use: applicants ask a health data access body for a data permit, with the main secondary-use provisions applying from around 2029. It does not displace data-protection law, which continues to apply alongside it.

q: A very large platform runs a recommender system driven by a large model. The division of labour between the DSA and the AI Act is that:
a: the AI Act applies to the model and displaces the DSA obligations in respect of that part of the service, which is treated as a product
b: the DSA governs the platform's systemic risks and recommender transparency, while the AI Act governs the AI system as a product
c: the DSA reaches only content moderation decisions, leaving recommender systems entirely to the AI Act
d: both apply, but the DSA prevails as lex specialis for any service designated as very large
explain: The two act cumulatively on different objects: service-level duties under the DSA, product-level duties under the AI Act. Neither displaces the other, so one recommender can be a DSA systemic-risk factor and an AI system within the AI Act's scope at the same time.

q: ChatGPT was designated a very large online search engine under the DSA on 31 August 2026. The consequence of that designation is that the provider must:
a: obtain a conformity assessment from a notified body before it may continue offering the service
b: appoint an authorised representative established in a Member State of the European Union within four months
c: assess and mitigate systemic risks, submit to independent audits and grant vetted researchers data access
d: register the service in the EU database of high-risk AI systems maintained by the Commission
explain: Designation follows from exceeding 45 million average monthly recipients in the Union and triggers Articles 34-37 DSA — systemic-risk assessment, mitigation, independent audit and researcher access — under Commission supervision, applying four months after notification (Art 33(6)). Registration in the AI Act database flows from high-risk classification under that separate regime, not from a DSA designation.

q: In 2026 the Commission referred several Member States to the Court of Justice over NIS2. That kind of referral is possible for NIS2 but not for the AI Act because:
a: NIS2 carries administrative fines, whereas the AI Act leaves the setting of penalties to national legislators
b: NIS2 is a directive requiring national transposition, whereas the AI Act is a regulation applying directly
c: enforcement of the AI Act is reserved to the Commission's AI Office rather than to the Court of Justice
d: cybersecurity is a shared competence, whereas the internal market is an exclusive competence of the Union
explain: Failure to transpose is a directive-specific infringement; a regulation needs no transposition, so no transposition deadline can be missed. Member States can still be pursued over the AI Act, but for failures such as not designating authorities.

q: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) imposes its obligations on:
a: manufacturers placing products with digital elements on the market of the European Union
b: online platforms with more than 45 million average monthly recipients of the service in the Union
c: essential and important entities in listed critical sectors, with accountability at management level
d: providers of general-purpose AI models above the systemic-risk training-compute threshold
explain: NIS2 is organisational cybersecurity: risk-management measures and incident reporting for entities across 18 sectors, with management bodies accountable. Product cybersecurity for digital products is the Cyber Resilience Act's object, not NIS2's.

q: The Cyber Resilience Act matters to an AI Act compliance team because:
a: it requires a fundamental rights impact assessment before a public body may deploy a product in its services
b: it requires essential and important entities in critical sectors to adopt cybersecurity risk-management measures
c: it sets lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, supporting Article 15 conformity
d: it obliges providers to register their high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market
explain: The CRA's secure-by-design, vulnerability-handling and update duties overlap with the AI Act's accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirement, so CRA evidence can serve Article 15. Reporting duties applied from 11 September 2026 and the full regime from 11 December 2027; risk management for entities in critical sectors is NIS2's object, not the CRA's.

q: Which is a target of the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030?
a: one AI Factory and one European Digital Innovation Hub in every Member State by 2030
b: 20 million ICT specialists employed in the Union, with more women entering the field
c: 50% of the electricity used by data centres in the Union to come from renewable sources
d: 75% of enterprises holding a cybersecurity certificate issued under the Cybersecurity Act
explain: Decision (EU) 2022/2481 sets 20 million ICT specialists, 80% of those aged 16-74 with at least basic digital skills, 75% of enterprises using cloud, big data or AI, gigabit connectivity and full online availability of key public services. The others are plausible policy goals but are not Digital Decade targets.

q: A draft note says the EU will miss its 2030 target of 75% of enterprises using cloud, AI or big data. The most technically sound caveat to add is:
a: the target applies only to large enterprises, so weak uptake among the small and micro firms that dominate the economy does not affect it
b: the target was withdrawn in the 2025 review, so no comparison against a benchmark is now possible
c: the indicator counts use of any one of three distinct technologies, so a single figure hides very different adoption rates
d: the indicator is collected by the Commission directly from firms, so national figures cannot be compared
explain: The target is a composite: an enterprise counts if it uses cloud computing, big data or AI, and cloud uptake is far higher than AI uptake, so the headline overstates AI diffusion. Eurostat's survey covers enterprises with ten or more employees across Member States and is comparable — the weakness lies in the composite, not the sampling.

q: The AI Continent Action Plan, COM(2025) 165 of 9 April 2025, is organised around:
a: harmonised standards, notified body capacity and a single conformity assessment procedure for high-risk systems placed on the market
b: computing infrastructure and data, adoption in strategic sectors, skills and talent, and regulatory simplification
c: a Union-owned foundation model, procurement quotas and mandatory open weights for public bodies
d: export controls on advanced processors, investment screening and reciprocity in public procurement
explain: The plan is a capacity-building agenda: AI Factories and Gigafactories, access to high-quality data, sectoral adoption, skills, and simplification of compliance. Standards and notified-body capacity are real AI Act workstreams but belong to implementation of the Regulation rather than to this plan.

q: AI Factories under the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking are:
a: private cloud regions contracted by Member States to host sensitive public administration workloads
b: AI-optimised supercomputing sites giving startups, SMEs and researchers compute alongside data and talent services
c: national testing and experimentation facilities certified to carry out conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems for SMEs
d: Commission-operated data centres hosting the Union's official registers and public sector language models
explain: AI Factories hosted at EuroHPC sites across most Member States, together with AI Factory Antennas, provide access to EuroHPC machines with wraparound services. Testing and experimentation facilities are a separate Digital Europe instrument aimed at sectoral testing, not at compute provision.

q: InvestAI, announced at the Paris AI Action Summit in February 2025, is:
a: a €2 billion instrument financing the national AI strategies coordinated through the Coordinated Plan on AI
b: a mobilisation of around €200 billion for AI investment, including a €20 billion fund for gigafactories
c: a €20 billion Union guarantee scheme covering liability claims arising from general-purpose AI models
d: a €200 billion budget line in the multiannual financial framework reserved for grants to AI research
explain: InvestAI combines public and private sources, with a dedicated €20 billion European fund intended to finance four AI gigafactories. It is not an MFF budget line: the money is leveraged from existing programmes, national contributions and private investors.

q: The Apply AI Strategy, COM(2025) 723 of 8 October 2025, aims primarily to:
a: accelerate uptake of AI in strategic sectors and in the public sector, supported by an Apply AI Alliance
b: create a European fund financing deployment of open-weight models inside Member State agencies
c: set out how AI will be used to accelerate scientific discovery across the European Research Area and its infrastructures
d: define the conformity assessment route for high-risk AI systems used by public administrations
explain: Apply AI is the adoption arm of the AI Continent agenda, mobilising around €1 billion from existing programmes across sectors such as health, manufacturing, energy and defence. The science agenda is the companion AI in Science strategy, COM(2025) 724, presented the same day.

q: RAISE, the initiative announced with the EU's AI in Science strategy, is:
a: a funding instrument financing chairs for AI researchers returning to the Union from third countries, and their teams
b: a pilot virtual institute pooling compute, data and expertise so that researchers can apply AI in science
c: a European register of scientific datasets made available for training general-purpose AI models
d: a research infrastructure consortium operating the Union's exascale supercomputers for open science
explain: RAISE is deliberately virtual: it federates existing resources rather than building a new physical institute, and it is the centrepiece of COM(2025) 724. The Union's exascale machines are operated by EuroHPC hosting entities, not by RAISE.

q: The Coordinated Plan on Artificial Intelligence differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: is a Council regulation setting national investment obligations on each Member State in AI research
b: is a non-binding framework aligning Member State strategies and investment, agreed in 2018 and revised in 2021
c: is an intergovernmental agreement outside the Union framework, like the Unified Patent Court system
d: is an implementing act laying down how national competent authorities coordinate market surveillance across borders
explain: The Coordinated Plan is soft coordination: joint priorities, national AI strategies and investment ambitions without legal obligation. Nothing in it binds a Member State — the binding layer arrived only with the AI Act.

q: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: applies only to public authorities and has no bearing on how private companies develop AI systems
b: is an international treaty open to non-European states, setting human-rights principles rather than product rules
c: is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights through individual applications lodged directly against the parties
d: was concluded by the Union alone and does not bind any Council of Europe member state directly
explain: The Convention sets principles for AI activities across their lifecycle and is open beyond Europe, with the United States and United Kingdom among the signatories. Private-sector activity is covered: each Party chooses between applying the Convention's principles to private actors or taking other appropriate measures, and must declare its choice.

q: Where an AI system processes personal data, the relationship between the GDPR and the AI Act is that:
a: the AI Act is lex specialis, so its data-governance rules replace the GDPR in respect of training data
b: both apply cumulatively, and compliance with the AI Act does not supply a lawful basis for the processing
c: the GDPR applies only where the system is classified as high-risk under Annex III of the AI Act
d: the AI Act covers non-personal data only, leaving personal data entirely to the data-protection regime
explain: The AI Act is product-safety legislation and leaves Union data-protection law untouched, so a controller still needs a lawful basis, purpose limitation and, where required, a DPIA. The lex specialis reading is the commonest error: Article 10's data-governance duties are additional to the GDPR, not a substitute for it.

q: Harmonised European standards matter to the AI Act's high-risk regime because:
a: Member States may not designate their market surveillance authorities until the standards are published
b: the Commission must withdraw from Annex III any use case for which no European standard has been developed
c: a notified body may certify a high-risk system only where a corresponding international ISO standard already exists
d: conformity with a standard cited in the Official Journal gives a presumption of conformity with the requirement
explain: Article 40 ties the presumption of conformity to standards cited in the Official Journal, which is why delay in the CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 work programme affects the whole high-risk timeline. Notified bodies can assess against the Act's requirements directly — a standard makes that cheaper and more predictable, it is not a precondition.

q: Compared with other jurisdictions, the AI Act's treatment of general-purpose AI models is distinctive because it:
a: imposes binding statutory duties on model providers where most comparable regimes still rely mainly on voluntary commitments
b: prohibits release of model weights above a defined training-compute threshold to any third party
c: requires model providers to obtain prior authorisation from a supervisory authority before any training run begins
d: applies only to models developed inside the Union, leaving imported models to national rules
explain: Chapter V is the first binding legal regime for model providers, covering documentation, copyright policy, training-content summaries and, above the systemic-risk threshold, evaluation and incident reporting. There is no ex-ante authorisation: obligations attach when a model is placed on the market, not before training.

q: In Commission usage, technological sovereignty in AI policy means:
a: reducing critical dependencies in compute, cloud and models by building Union capacity while staying open
b: giving Union-based providers preference in the public procurement of cloud and AI services
c: requiring that data generated within the Union be stored and processed on Union territory by Union-based providers
d: screening every foreign direct investment in companies developing general-purpose AI models
explain: The concept is capacity and resilience — the Chips Act, EuroHPC and AI Factories, InvestAI — and the Commission consistently frames it as open strategic autonomy rather than autarky. Data localisation is a much narrower measure the Union has largely avoided in its data legislation.

q: The EU's answer to AI-generated disinformation combines:
a: mandatory provenance certificates for all online media, with strict liability for hosting providers
b: criminal penalties under Union law with takedown orders issued directly by the European Commission
c: transparency duties on the content's provider under the AI Act with systemic-risk mitigation by platforms under the DSA
d: an obligation on search engines and social platforms to demote synthetic content, with fines under the Digital Markets Act
explain: Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of synthetic content by the provider and disclosure of deep fakes by the deployer, while Articles 34-35 DSA make manipulated content a systemic risk platforms must mitigate, operationalised through the Code of Conduct on Disinformation. There is no Union criminal-law layer and no Commission takedown power for this content.

q: A ministry wants EU co-funding to set up AI testing facilities and advanced digital skills courses. The instrument designed for that is:
a: Horizon Europe, which funds collaborative research and innovation projects across the whole of the Union and beyond
b: the Recovery and Resilience Facility, which finances national reform and investment milestones
c: the Connecting Europe Facility, which finances cross-border digital and transport infrastructure
d: the Digital Europe Programme, which funds deployment capacity, testing facilities, skills and data spaces
explain: Digital Europe is the deployment programme: AI testing and experimentation facilities, European Digital Innovation Hubs, advanced digital skills and data spaces. Horizon Europe is the closest alternative but funds research and innovation rather than the roll-out of capacity.

q: A minister asks whether the EU rolled back its AI rules in 2026. The most accurate answer is that the Commission:
a: withdrew the AI Act and replaced it with a voluntary code negotiated with the main model providers
b: transferred enforcement to the Member States and gave up the Commission's own supervisory powers
c: suspended application of the whole Act until harmonised European standards are cited in the Official Journal of the Union
d: deferred the high-risk obligations and lightened documentation duties, keeping prohibitions and GPAI rules in force
explain: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed Annex III duties to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028 and simplified documentation, but Article 5 and Chapter V continued to apply and the Commission retained its GPAI enforcement powers. Simplification changed timing and burden, not the substance of the prohibitions.

q: Which body acts as market surveillance authority for AI systems used by the Union's own institutions, bodies and agencies?
a: the national authority of the Member State in which the institution has its seat
b: the European AI Board, acting through its standing subgroup on market surveillance
c: the AI Office, which supervises Union bodies as well as general-purpose model providers
d: the European Data Protection Supervisor, which may also fine Union institutions and bodies
explain: Article 74(9) designates the EDPS for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the Act's scope, with fining powers under Article 100. The AI Office is the tempting answer, but its direct supervisory mandate covers general-purpose AI models, not the institutions' own use of AI systems.

q: Advanced AI developers report voluntarily against an agreed transparency framework hosted by the OECD. That framework belongs to:
a: the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI, which collects developer disclosures from participating firms
b: the Council of Europe Framework Convention, whose parties report on implementation every two years
c: the Global Partnership on AI, whose member states publish national compliance reports each year
d: the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, whose reporting framework companies began using in February 2025
explain: The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework, launched in February 2025 and hosted by the OECD, lets organisations developing advanced AI report against the G7 International Code of Conduct. The Council of Europe Convention is a state-level treaty and imposes no reporting duty on companies.

q: Under the AI Act, a provider releasing a model under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters:
a: gains the relief only where the model stays below the transparency threshold set out in Annex XI
b: must notify the AI Office before release so that a systemic-risk screening can be carried out
c: falls outside the Regulation's scope entirely, since nothing is placed on the Union market in return for payment
d: is relieved of the technical documentation duties but keeps the copyright policy and training-content summary
explain: Article 53(2) lifts the technical documentation and downstream-information duties for genuinely open releases, but the copyright policy and public training-content summary always apply, and the relief falls away entirely for models with systemic risk. Openness is a burden reduction, not a scope exclusion.

q: Which mapping of instrument to its primary object is correct throughout?
a: Data Act to public sector data re-use; DGA to secondary use of health data; EHDS to cloud switching; DMA to independent platform audits
b: AI Act to chip supply; Chips Act to AI conformity; DGA to cloud switching; DSA to incident reporting
c: DSA to data intermediation; DGA to platform moderation; CRA to gatekeeper conduct; NIS2 to product safety
d: DMA to gatekeeper contestability; NIS2 to organisational cybersecurity; CRA to product cybersecurity; Data Act to connected-product data
explain: Each pairing in the key matches the instrument's core object. The DSA governs intermediary services and platform duties while the DGA sets up data intermediation and altruism — swapping those two is the commonest mix-up.

q: A national immigration authority plans to deploy an AI system to triage visa applications. Before putting it into use it must:
a: have the system certified by a notified body established in the Member State of deployment
b: publish the system's technical documentation and the datasets used to train and validate it
c: obtain an opinion from the European AI Board and register the system in a national database of public deployments
d: carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment and operate under its market surveillance authority
explain: Migration, asylum and border control is an Annex III area, and public bodies deploying such systems owe the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, under the national market surveillance authority (for Union bodies it would be the EDPS, Art 74(9)). A notified body is not generally required — most Annex III systems use internal control for conformity assessment.

q: Signing the general-purpose AI Code of Practice:
a: is mandatory for any provider whose model exceeds the systemic-risk training-compute threshold
b: replaces the Chapter V obligations for signatories until harmonised standards become available
c: has been a condition for placing a general-purpose AI model on the market of the Union since August 2025
d: is voluntary and gives signatories a recognised route to demonstrate compliance with Chapter V duties
explain: Adherence is voluntary: the Commission assessed the Code as an adequate means of demonstrating compliance, and non-signatories must show compliance by other means, which invites closer scrutiny. Meta declined to sign, and xAI signed only the Safety and Security chapter — both remain lawful positions.

q: The mechanism by which the Commission can add a use case to Annex III of the AI Act is:
a: an amendment through the ordinary legislative procedure proposed jointly with the Council
b: a delegated act, confined to the areas already listed and conditional on evidence of risk
c: a Commission decision published in the Official Journal after a public consultation
d: an implementing act adopted after a favourable opinion of the European AI Board
explain: Article 7 empowers delegated acts, which keeps the high-risk list adaptable without reopening the Regulation, but the Commission cannot create a new Annex III area. Implementing acts are used elsewhere in the Act — for the Scientific Panel's rules, for instance — which makes that option the plausible trap.

q: The AI Gigafactory programme required a change to EuroHPC's founding regulation because:
a: the Joint Undertaking's mandate had to be extended to cover AI infrastructure of this scale and purpose
b: state aid clearance could not be granted without an explicit legal base in a Council regulation
c: supercomputer procurement had to be moved from national authorities to the Joint Undertaking itself
d: the Union's own resources ceiling had to be raised to accommodate the additional capital expenditure
explain: Council Regulation (EU) 2026/150 of 16 January 2026 amended Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 so that EuroHPC could host and procure gigafactory-scale AI infrastructure. The Joint Undertaking already procured supercomputers jointly with participating states, so no transfer of procurement competence was needed.

q: The legal basis on which general-purpose model providers currently rely for text and data mining of protected works is:
a: the Database Directive's sui generis right, which permits extraction for non-commercial research purposes
b: the Data Act's provisions on access to data generated by connected products and related services
c: the exceptions in the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive, subject to a reservation of rights
d: a dedicated exception in the AI Act covering training of general-purpose models on lawfully accessed works
explain: Articles 3 and 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 supply the text and data mining exceptions, and Article 4's machine-readable opt-out is what rightsholders use to reserve their works. The AI Act adds a duty to have a copyright policy respecting that reservation, but creates no exception of its own — assuming otherwise is the common error.

q: Which statement about AI and EU competition policy is accurate?
a: acquisitions of model developers escape merger control entirely because the targets have little turnover
b: the Commission may impose interoperability duties on model providers without any finding of dominance
c: partnerships between large platforms and model developers can be reviewed even short of a notifiable merger
d: designation under the Digital Markets Act extends automatically to every AI service a gatekeeper offers
explain: The Commission has examined big-tech and model-lab arrangements under merger and antitrust tools, precisely because compute-for-equity structures often fall outside notification thresholds. DMA designation is service by service: an AI assistant is covered only if it is designated as, or integrated into, a designated core platform service.

q: Under the AI Act's penalty regime, the highest tier of administrative fines applies to:
a: failure to register a high-risk system in the EU database, up to €30 million or 6% of worldwide turnover
b: supply of incorrect information to notified bodies, up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover
c: infringement of the prohibited practices in Article 5, up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover
d: failure by a deployer to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment, up to 6% of annual turnover
explain: Article 99 reserves the 7% or €35 million ceiling for breaches of Article 5, with most other infringements at 3% or €15 million and supplying incorrect information at 1% or €7.5 million. The distractor figures echo the GDPR's tiers, which do not map onto the AI Act.

q: European Digital Innovation Hubs are:
a: one-stop shops co-funded by the Union helping SMEs and public bodies test digital and AI technology before investing
b: consortia operating the Union's AI Factories and allocating supercomputing time to researchers
c: accredited bodies carrying out conformity assessment of AI systems for SMEs at reduced fees
d: regional offices of the AI Office supervising high-risk AI systems used on their territory and advising national authorities
explain: The EDIH network is the test-before-invest retail layer of EU digital policy, co-funded by the Digital Europe Programme and national sources (151 hubs selected in the 2021-22 calls; 83 renewed in October 2025). Compute access is the AI Factories' role — EDIHs advise, train and broker finance rather than operate infrastructure.

q: The AI Act's obligations were staged so that:
a: all obligations applied together two years after entry into force, as in other internal market regulations
b: prohibitions and AI literacy applied first, general-purpose model duties next, and high-risk duties last
c: each Member State fixed its own application dates within a window laid down by the Regulation
d: the high-risk duties applied first, because they had the clearest precedent in existing product legislation
explain: Article 113 stages application: prohibitions and AI literacy six months after entry into force, general-purpose AI and governance at twelve months, with the high-risk regime last — and pushed further out by the Digital Omnibus. Dates are fixed by the Regulation itself, leaving no national discretion.

q: Under the Safety and Security chapter of the general-purpose AI Code of Practice, a safety and security framework is expected to set out:
a: a commitment to release model weights openly once independent evaluations have been concluded
b: risk acceptance criteria tied to capability thresholds, with mitigations and a decision on whether to proceed
c: a guarantee that model weights and inference operations remain within Union territory at all times
d: an insurance arrangement covering damage to third parties arising from downstream deployment of the model by others
explain: The framework is a pre-committed decision procedure keyed to measured capability: tiers defined in terms of model capabilities, a safety margin, and an explicit determination whether to proceed with development or with making the model available. It is neither a financial nor a localisation undertaking.

q: The most defensible statement for a 2026 policy brief on AI and the EU labour market is:
a: net displacement will exceed job creation in every Member State and every sector before 2030
b: labour-market effects fall outside Union competence and cannot be addressed at Union level
c: exposure concentrates in cognitive and clerical tasks, with evidence clearer on task composition than on net jobs
d: productivity gains fully offset displacement, so aggregate employment effects can safely be disregarded in planning
explain: That is the honest reading of the current evidence base: occupational exposure measures are reasonably robust, while net employment effects remain contested and vary by sector and Member State. The other options either overclaim a uniform outcome or deny competences the Union plainly has in skills and social policy.

q: An EU note on AI's environmental footprint should draw its reporting data primarily from:
a: harmonised standards adopted under the AI Act covering the energy efficiency of high-risk systems and their training
b: product documentation required under the Cyber Resilience Act for products with digital elements
c: the data-centre reporting scheme under the Energy Efficiency Directive plus energy information in GPAI documentation
d: annual sustainability reports published voluntarily by the largest cloud and AI model providers
