explain: Those are the two mandatory channels: data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT power report annually to the European database under the Energy Efficiency Directive, and Annex XI of the AI Act requires the known or estimated energy consumption of a general-purpose model. Provider sustainability reports are useful but voluntary, unaudited and not comparable across firms.

q: A tax administration ranks returns for audit selection using an AI system. The most accurate AI Act reading is:
a: outside the Act's scope, because direct taxation remains within Member State competence alone
b: prohibited, because it predicts the likelihood of an offence on the basis of profiling alone
c: not listed in Annex III, so the deployer must still test it against Article 5, data-protection and administrative law
d: high-risk, because Annex III covers any AI system that a public authority deploys in the exercise of its official duties
explain: Tax audit selection is not an Annex III use case — tax authorities are not law enforcement authorities for this purpose — so the compliance burden comes from elsewhere. The Article 5 prohibition on predicting criminal offences is the tempting reading, but it is confined to assessing the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence.

q: Which risk is one of the specified systemic risks that a signatory of the general-purpose AI Code of Practice must always assess, with no prior screening step?
a: infringement of copyright in the works used to train and subsequently fine-tune the model
b: concentration of the market for advanced general-purpose AI models among a handful of providers
c: loss of control over a model that can evade human oversight or resist being modified
d: energy consumption of large-scale training runs and of high-volume inference serving at scale
explain: The Safety and Security chapter names four specified systemic risks — chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear; loss of control; cyber offence; harmful manipulation — which are identified automatically rather than through screening. Concentration of power and environmental effects sit in the open-ended identification process built on the five broader risk types, so they are assessed only where screening selects them.

q: A signatory's safety and security framework must define systemic risk acceptance criteria. For a specified systemic risk, those criteria are required to be:
a: reviewed each year by an independent auditor accredited by a national notifying authority
b: expressed as measurable tiers of model capability, including at least one tier the model has not reached
c: agreed in advance with the AI Office and published in full before training of the model is allowed to begin
d: derived from the compute used in training, measured against the threshold set in Article 51
explain: The Code requires tiers defined in terms of capabilities, measurable, with a safety margin and at least one unreached tier, so the provider commits in advance to a decision point rather than judging after the fact. The criteria are the provider's own: the Commission assesses the adequacy of the Code, it does not approve individual frameworks before training.

q: A draft measure would treat any model trained above a fixed floating-point-operations threshold as high risk and anything below it as safe. The strongest technical objection is:
a: the threshold would capture only models trained inside the Union, leaving imported models unregulated
b: capability per unit of compute rises with algorithmic progress, so a fixed threshold drifts from the risk it proxies
c: training compute cannot be measured after the fact, so the threshold would be impossible to enforce
d: compute figures are commercially sensitive, so providers could not disclose them without suffering competitive harm
explain: A compute threshold is a decaying proxy: the same capability becomes reachable with less compute each year, and fine-tuning or scaffolding adds capability without additional training compute. The AI Act treats 10^25 operations as a rebuttable presumption and lets the Commission amend it by delegated act precisely because the proxy needs maintenance.

q: A draft policy states that mandatory watermarking of AI-generated images will solve the deepfake problem. The most technically sound critique is:
a: watermarks can be stripped or degraded, and their absence cannot be read as evidence that content is authentic
b: watermarking is incompatible with the transparency obligations already imposed under Article 50
c: watermarking works only for still images, so audio and video content could not be covered by the measure at all
d: watermarking would expose the confidentiality of the model weights used to produce the content
explain: Detection fails in both directions: adversaries remove or forge marks, and the volume of unmarked legitimate content means absence of a mark proves nothing, so provenance has to be paired with platform-level mitigation and media literacy. Audio and video can in fact be marked, and the Article 50 duty already extends to them.

q: A draft rule would require every output of a deep neural network to be accompanied by a complete causal explanation of how it was produced. The soundest objection is:
a: no such explanation exists for models of this kind, so the rule would be met only by post-hoc approximations
b: explanations would expose the training data and so conflict with data-protection and trade-secret obligations
c: generating explanations at inference time would raise the energy cost of each query substantially
d: the requirement duplicates the technical documentation already owed under Annex XI of the AI Act
explain: Attribution methods approximate a model's behaviour and can disagree with one another, so a completeness requirement would be satisfied in form rather than substance. The workable drafting is the AI Act's: information meaningful for the intended purpose and for the person affected, backed by logging and human oversight.

q: A Member State proposes that all AI inference for public bodies run on servers in its territory, so as to guarantee control over the models used. The main gap in that reasoning is:
a: the location of inference says nothing about who controls the weights, the updates or the model's withdrawal
b: inference cannot be run on national infrastructure unless the provider discloses its source code
c: national servers cannot reach the throughput large models need without dedicated accelerators
d: restricting the location of processing is incompatible with the free movement of data within the internal market
explain: Hosting determines where computation happens; it confers no rights over the model itself, so a provider can still deprecate a version, change behaviour through an update or end the licence. Control is secured contractually — version pinning, exit rights, escrow — and by access to weights, not by geography.

q: For technology watch on open-weight models, the distinctive feature compared with models served only through an API is that:
a: open-weight models are always smaller and so stay below the systemic-risk compute threshold
b: safeguards can be removed by fine-tuning after release, and a release cannot be recalled once weights circulate
c: the provider keeps a technical means of revoking access if the model is later found to be unsafe
d: downstream users become providers under the AI Act as soon as they run the model on their own hardware rather than an interface
explain: Irreversibility is the defining property: refusal training can be undone cheaply, and no update or shutdown reaches copies already distributed, which is why the Act's open-source relief falls away at systemic-risk scale. Running a model on your own hardware does not by itself make you a provider — that turns on substantial modification or placing it on the market under your own name.

q: The International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, is best described to a non-technical audience as:
a: a negotiated intergovernmental text setting out the specific commitments that the participating states have accepted
b: a synthesis of scientific evidence on advanced AI risks that deliberately makes no policy recommendations
c: the technical annex to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on artificial intelligence
d: an annual compliance assessment of the largest model providers against agreed safety benchmarks
explain: The Report is an evidence synthesis backed by around thirty countries plus the EU, OECD and UN, and its authors stress that policy choices are for governments. Presenting it as an agreed government position is the error most likely to mislead a policy audience.

q: In technology watch on the general-purpose AI ecosystem, which observation is the most robust basis for concern about concentration?
a: training costs have fallen far enough that a mid-sized firm could now train a frontier model of its own
b: the number of general-purpose AI models released each year has fallen steadily since 2023
c: frontier training depends on a small number of accelerator suppliers and hyperscale cloud operators
d: most of the world's most capable models are now developed inside the European Union
explain: Supply of advanced accelerators and of hyperscale training capacity is genuinely narrow, and that structural fact is what EU compute policy responds to. Model releases have risen rather than fallen, and frontier training runs remain well beyond a mid-sized firm's reach even though inference and fine-tuning costs have dropped sharply.

q: A provider of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk finds that the model enabled a significant cyber intrusion. Under the AI Act it must:
a: track and document the incident and report it without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national authorities
b: notify the national market surveillance authority of every Member State concerned within fifteen days
c: suspend availability of the model until the Commission has completed an evaluation of that model
d: inform the European Data Protection Supervisor and notify the affected data subjects directly
explain: Article 55(1)(c) routes serious-incident reporting for systemic-risk models to the AI Office without undue delay, with national competent authorities informed as appropriate. The fifteen-day deadline belongs to Article 73, which applies to providers of high-risk AI systems reporting to market surveillance authorities.

q: A briefing on AI's energy footprint should note that, for a widely used model across its lifetime:
a: training dominates lifetime energy use, so limiting the size of training runs is the decisive lever
b: cumulative inference can exceed the energy used for training, so deployment scale matters as much as model size
c: energy use is proportional to parameter count, so a published parameter count suffices for an estimate
d: data-centre electricity consumption is already capped for operators reporting under the Energy Efficiency Directive
explain: High-volume serving accumulates demand that can outweigh a single training run, which is why the policy levers include data-centre efficiency and demand-side measures rather than training alone. The Energy Efficiency Directive imposes reporting on data centres above 500 kW of installed IT power, not a cap on their consumption.

q: Under the DSA, the Commission's guidelines on electoral integrity ask very large platforms to:
a: remove all synthetic media during the period between the calling of an election and the close of polling stations
b: label generative AI content in political contexts and apply provenance techniques such as watermarking and metadata
c: verify the identity of every account that posts political content during an electoral campaign
d: obtain approval from national electoral authorities for recommender changes made during a campaign
explain: The April 2024 guidelines under Article 35(3) recommend labelling and provenance signals that survive resharing, including labels on AI-generated political advertising. They stop short of removal duties or identity verification, which would raise fundamental-rights problems of their own.

q: The Commission's July 2025 guidelines on the protection of minors under the DSA were accompanied by:
a: a prohibition on using recommender systems for accounts belonging to users under eighteen
b: an open-source age-verification blueprint built on the European Digital Identity Wallet architecture
c: a mandatory minimum age of sixteen for access to social media services across the Union
d: a delegated act laying down binding design standards for services that are likely to be accessed by minors
explain: The guidelines under Article 28(4) came with a white-label age-verification application built on the EUDI Wallet technical architecture and piloted by several Member States. No EU-wide minimum age was set: the guidelines recommend how to apply Article 28(1) and are not binding standards.

q: For an AI-driven customer service interface offered to consumers in the Union, accessibility obligations arise principally from:
a: the General Product Safety Regulation, which covers consumer products placed on the Union market
b: the European Accessibility Act, applicable since June 2025 to e-commerce, banking and consumer computing
c: Directive (EU) 2016/2102, on the accessibility of public sector websites and mobile applications
d: the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to design their interfaces free of dark patterns
explain: The European Accessibility Act sets accessibility requirements for consumer-facing products and services, including e-commerce and consumer banking, and has applied since 28 June 2025. The public sector website directive is the close alternative but reaches only public sector bodies' sites and apps.

q: The latest State of the Digital Decade report projects that the Union will fall several million short of its 20 million ICT specialists target by 2030. The most defensible inference is:
a: the gap will close by itself as AI tools reduce the skills needed for information technology work
b: the shortfall lies in graduate flows and reskilling capacity, so it will not close through employer demand alone
c: the target should be revised downward, because the projection shows it was set unrealistically high
d: the measurement excludes self-employed specialists, so the true figure is in reality already close to the target
explain: The State of the Digital Decade 2026 report (17 June 2026) counts around 10.5 million ICT specialists employed in 2025 and projects about 12.2 million by 2030 — a gap of roughly 7.8 million that reflects the supply of trained people rather than weak demand. The target is fixed in Decision (EU) 2022/2481 and can be changed only by amending it, so treating a missed projection as a reason to restate the ambition confuses measurement with policy.

q: A national AI strategy promises a sovereign foundation model, a public compute cluster and a dedicated ministry, but names no evaluation criteria, no procurement route and no budget beyond year two. Its weakest element is:
a: the choice to train a national model rather than fine-tune an existing open-weight model
b: the creation of a dedicated ministry rather than assigning AI policy to an existing government department
c: the absence of any means to judge whether the investment worked or to sustain it beyond the pilot
d: reliance on public compute when commercial cloud capacity could be procured far more quickly
explain: A strategy without success criteria or a funding path beyond the pilot can be neither steered nor defended, and that failure holds whatever technical choices it makes. The other three describe genuine trade-offs, each defensible depending on the country's industrial base and talent pool.

q: A company's responsible-AI policy promises human oversight of all AI decisions, internal red-teaming before each release and an ethics board meeting once a year. The most technically sound criticism is:
a: internal red-teaming is worthless unless carried out by an accredited external conformity assessment body
b: an ethics board is unnecessary where the company already complies with the Union's data-protection rules
c: oversight of every decision is not credible at scale and invites rubber-stamping rather than genuine control
d: the policy should commit to publishing model weights so that independent researchers can verify its claims
explain: A blanket oversight promise fails the way automation bias does: volume forces nominal review, so the credible commitment is oversight targeted at consequential decisions with measured override rates. Internal red-teaming is a recognised practice — its weaknesses are scope and independence, not the absence of accreditation.

q: Comparing approaches to AI governance as of 2026, which statement is accurate?
a: China regulates generative AI only through voluntary standards agreed with domestic providers
b: the United Kingdom enacted a general AI statute after renaming its AI Security Institute
c: the United States has no cross-cutting federal AI statute and acts mainly through executive orders
d: the Council of Europe Framework Convention has entered into force and now binds all of its signatories
explain: US federal policy has run through executive orders and an AI action plan since January 2025, with Congress passing no cross-cutting legislation. The Council of Europe Convention is the closest trap, but it binds only Parties that have ratified it — signature alone creates no obligation to apply its terms.

q: After the Digital Omnibus, the AI Act's regulatory sandbox regime requires that:
a: sandboxes be operated jointly by the AI Office and the national data protection authorities
b: providers test high-risk systems in a sandbox before any conformity assessment may be carried out
c: each Member State establish at least one national sandbox by 2 August 2027, with a Union-level sandbox possible
d: participation in a sandbox exempt the provider from the high-risk obligations for a period of up to three years
explain: The Omnibus moved the national sandbox deadline from 2 August 2026 to 2 August 2027 and added a Union-level sandbox that the AI Office may establish, with priority access for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps. A sandbox is voluntary supervised testing: it neither replaces conformity assessment nor suspends obligations.

q: The Digital Omnibus added new entries to the AI Act's list of prohibited practices. They concern:
a: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, without judicial authorisation
b: generating or manipulating intimate imagery of an identifiable person without consent, and abuse material involving children
c: emotion recognition in the workplace and in educational institutions outside medical or safety uses
d: untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet to build facial recognition databases
explain: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 inserted prohibitions on non-consensual intimate imagery and on child sexual abuse material into Article 5(1), applicable from 2 December 2026. The other three practices have been prohibited since February 2025, which is what makes them plausible answers.

q: A ministry uses an AI system that flags inconsistencies in benefit decisions already taken, for human review, without scoring or ranking applicants. Under the AI Act the system:
a: is automatically high risk because it is used by a public authority in the exercise of its duties
b: is outside the Regulation altogether, because the final decision is always taken by a human official
c: is prohibited, because it evaluates natural persons on the basis of their social or personal behaviour over a period
d: may fall outside the high-risk class under the derogation, but must be registered and must not involve profiling
explain: Article 6(3) lets an Annex III system escape the high-risk class where it detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, but profiling of natural persons always remains high risk and the assessment must be documented and the system registered. Deployment by a public authority is not itself the trigger — the use case has to sit in Annex III.

q: Presenting a model evaluation to a non-technical audience, the most honest way to convey uncertainty around a reported 92% accuracy is to:
a: compare the figure with human performance on the same task, giving the audience a familiar reference
b: round the figure down to 90% so that the audience does not overinterpret the precision of the result
c: present only the confidence interval, so that the audience sees a statistical range rather than a point
d: state the test conditions and the population it was measured on, and say where it is likely to be worse
explain: A headline metric means something only with its test set, its population and its known failure modes, which is what lets a policy audience judge whether it transfers to their setting. A human baseline is a useful device but says nothing about where the model's errors fall and misleads if it was measured under different conditions.

q: Designing AI awareness training for policy officers who will not build systems, the most useful learning objective is:
a: operating the main commercial chat assistants and comparing their outputs on policy tasks
b: being able to implement a transformer architecture and train it on a small labelled dataset
c: memorising the article numbers of the AI Act's obligations for providers and for deployers
d: recognising when a claim about an AI system needs evidence, and what evidence would settle it
explain: Article 4 requires competence proportionate to role, and for policy staff the transferable skill is critical appraisal of claims rather than engineering or recitation. Hands-on use of assistants builds familiarity but does not by itself teach anyone to judge whether a vendor's performance claim is sound.

q: An SME asks where to obtain authoritative guidance on whether its product falls within the AI Act. The service created for that purpose is:
a: the European Digital Innovation Hub network, which advises SMEs on adopting digital technologies
b: the Scientific Panel of Independent Experts, which advises on general-purpose AI model risks
c: the European AI Board, which issues opinions on consistent application of the Regulation
d: the AI Act Service Desk and single information platform, the Commission's single entry point for AI Act questions
explain: The Service Desk is the single entry point for AI Act questions, with an explorer, a compliance checker and a helpdesk aimed at SMEs and start-ups. EDIHs advise on adoption and the AI Board coordinates national authorities — neither answers an individual firm's classification question.

q: The Data Union Strategy presented in November 2025 responds to which diagnosis?
a: European data centres lack the capacity to store the datasets needed for frontier model training
b: Member States apply divergent data localisation requirements to public sector information holdings
c: data-protection rules prevent any use of European personal data for machine learning purposes
d: the Union's data rules are fragmented and high-quality data is hard to access for training AI models
explain: The strategy targets simplification and consolidation of the data acquis plus better availability of high-quality data for AI, on the view that complexity and fragmentation are the binding constraint. Storage capacity is a separate problem addressed by the compute and cloud strand of the AI Continent agenda.

q: The Cloud and AI Development Act, as proposed by the Commission in 2026, would:
a: set binding energy efficiency limits for data centres above a defined installed power threshold
b: require providers of general-purpose AI models to host their model weights on infrastructure located in the Union
c: oblige Member States to procure compute capacity exclusively through the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking
d: expand Union data-centre capacity and add a cloud sovereignty framework conditioning public procurement
explain: The proposal aims to multiply EU data-centre capacity and to create assurance levels for cloud sovereignty that gate public-sector procurement, with Union added value as a non-price award criterion. It is a proposal in the ordinary legislative procedure, not law, and imposes no localisation duty on model providers.
